title: All Blacks coach Dave Rennie expresses his dismay at 'crazy' World Cup draw
summary: The All Blacks coach is unhappy with a Rugby World Cup draw that could pit his side against the Springboks as early as the quarter-finals.
long_summary:
All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has criticised the draw for next year's Rugby World Cup. If the expected results hold, New Zealand could meet South Africa in the quarter-finals, which would knock out one of the two strongest teams before the semi-finals. Rennie compared this to 2023, when four of the world's top sides met in the quarters, and said the bracket was once again poorly arranged.

The draw also places New Zealand and Australia in the same pool, the first time the two former champions have met in pool play at a World Cup. Rennie accepted that winning the title means beating every opponent regardless, and the All Blacks open against Chile on 2 October. Before that, they face the Wallabies in Sydney in a match that has no bearing on the Bledisloe Cup, which New Zealand already keeps for another year. Rennie expects a motivated Australian side playing in front of a large home crowd.

Rennie also defended his squad's recovery after a seven-week tour of South Africa, which ended in a 3-1 series defeat to the Springboks. He said critics who wanted the players sent straight into domestic competition overlooked the physical and emotional strain of the trip. Damian McKenzie has retained the first five-eighth role after a strong performance at Eden Park, and he spoke about balancing kicking and running while still directing the team's game management. He expects a tough response from the Wallabies.

title: Auckland FC defend controversial Sam Cosgrove call ahead of A-League season opener
summary: Auckland FC's English striker was sent off in an Intercontinental Cup match in August. The club says he served his two-match ban in National League games, and is standing by the call before the A-League season opens.
long_summary:
Auckland FC have defended their decision to select English striker Sam Cosgrove for the opening A-League match against Melbourne City on Saturday. Cosgrove was sent off in the club's Intercontinental Cup game in August and was due a two-match ban. The club's director of football, Terry McFlynn, says FIFA's notice required the suspension to be served in the club's next two official matches, and because National League fixtures count as official, Cosgrove served it there.

McFlynn said Auckland would apply the same process to any player in that situation. Cosgrove was joint golden boot winner last season with 12 goals. Four of the club's five permitted visa spots are filled, including captain Hiroki Sakai from Japan, Chilean midfielder Felipe Gallegos and Norwegian Daniel Normann, with the fifth expected to be signed within a week. Auckland are also looking for a winger to replace Jesse Randall, who scored nine goals last season and has left the club.

The league has tighter spending limits this season. McFlynn argued Auckland had handled the change particularly well and rejected claims that the salary cap had been changed specifically for the club as it enters its third year. He said the club will keep searching globally for players who can strengthen team culture.

The squad also relies on younger players, which McFlynn believes strengthens the competition and brings energy to the league. He framed the changes as an opportunity rather than a setback. The story matters because it raises questions about how suspension rules are applied across competitions and how clubs adapt under a tighter salary cap.

title: The Memory Shortage Comes for Schools
summary: School districts are struggling to pay for all their pupils' Chromebooks as a shortage of memory chips drives up the cost of hardware.
long_summary:
A global shortage of memory chips, driven largely by demand from the AI industry, is raising the price of consumer electronics and squeezing school districts that buy computers in bulk. The reporting focuses on Chromebooks and tablets, which are now standard for nearly every student in the United States. Prices have climbed steeply since 2023, and districts have been forced to find extra money or change plans.

The piece draws on interviews with technology directors and officials. Steve Richardson of Homewood-Flossmoor High School in Illinois described his district's Chromebook cost rising from about 353 dollars to over 500 dollars, and the district skipped buying new whiteboards and teacher computers as a result. Chatham County Schools in North Carolina and Loudoun County Public Schools in Virginia have also reported higher costs and vendor quotes that now expire within days. Dorann Avey of the State Educational Technology Directors Association warned that the shortage could widen the digital divide, and an executive at Micron warned that no end to the shortage is in sight.

Districts are responding in several ways. Some are stretching laptop lifespans from about four years to seven or eight, which raises cybersecurity concerns because older machines may not run current operating systems. Others are considering ending one-to-one device policies or asking students to bring their own devices. The shortage also reaches servers that run security cameras, badge readers and logins, so schools may have to rethink many technology purchases.

The story matters because it shows how a supply problem in the AI sector can ripple down to public institutions. Schools that already had tight budgets must now decide which technology actually improves learning and which they can no longer afford, with consequences for students' access to digital tools and for school security.

title: This Is Edgar Allan Poe, and I Am Begging Kelly Clarkson to Take My Bird
summary: A comic letter from Edgar Allan Poe, pleading with Kelly Clarkson to give his raven a new home.
long_summary:
This is a satirical letter written in the voice of Edgar Allan Poe, addressed to singer Kelly Clarkson. Poe's narrator wants to offload a raven that has settled uninvited on a bust of Pallas in his home. He has read about Clarkson's wish for a pet bird, which was blocked, and about her encounter with the toy store Art of Play, which sells a windup bird she had been interested in. He proposes a trade.

The narrator describes how the raven arrived, tapping at his door on a gloomy night in an echo of his famous poem. He has tried to shoo it out and even opened a window, but the bird refuses to leave and only repeats a single word at intervals. He pitches it to Clarkson as a decor-friendly pet that suits any room, offers the bust as a sweetener, and says he would accept payment, which could help him remove a beating heart under his floorboards.

The piece ends with a note that the writer first placed the heart in the wall by mistake, and that Alexandra Petri gets the detail right in the Poe chapter of her book. The letter is a playful jab at the literary legend and at celebrity news, and it is written as a message that never really expects a reply.

title: Bringing GPT-Rosalind to academic research labs
summary: Under a new Rosalind Academic Plan, OpenAI is giving eligible university labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and its tools for life sciences research.
long_summary:
OpenAI has launched the Rosalind Academic Plan, which gives eligible university labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind, its specialised life sciences model, and the Rosalind Workbench. The workbench coordinates specialised tools for areas such as medicinal chemistry, genomics and wet-lab work. Eligible labs can get up to 30 seats on OpenAI's Business Standard tier at no cost for up to 12 months, along with access to OpenAI's other commercially available frontier models, subject to usage limits. API access is not included for now. GPT-Rosalind itself requires separate trusted-access approval.

The plan is currently open only to academic labs at U.S. universities. Principal investigators or lab leads can apply directly, or labs at institutions that already have an OpenAI Enterprise agreement must apply through that route. Before activation, OpenAI checks the institution's legitimacy, the lead's identity and appointment, and the lab's research and intended use. Monitoring and enforcement continue after activation, and OpenAI may follow up with researchers on sensitive work. Research data shared through the plan is not used to train models by default.

OpenAI presents the plan as support for basic academic research, which it says has historically led to advances such as the Human Genome Project, CRISPR-Cas9 and mRNA vaccines. The company says the plan aims to help scientists work on drug and protein design and on questions such as neurodegeneration, and it ties the initiative to its goal of making artificial general intelligence benefit all of humanity.

The move matters because it lowers the cost of advanced AI for academic scientists, who often lack the budgets of industry labs. It also shows how a leading AI company is positioning its specialised models for sensitive biological research, with access gated by vetting and safeguards. Whether the benefits reach labs beyond the initial U.S. eligibility pool remains to be seen.

title: Scientists discover an ancient shipwreck dating to when the Great Pyramid was built
summary: A wreck found on the seabed off the coast of Türkiye, its cargo still largely intact, is thought to be between 4,400 and 4,700 years old.
long_summary:
Researchers at Akdeniz University in Türkiye found a small vessel on the Mediterranean seabed in 2024 after a sonar reading picked it up. Three stone anchors lay around the wreck. The scientists date the boat to the early Bronze Age, roughly 4,400 to 4,700 years ago, which would make it the oldest shipwreck found so far. Most wrecks in the region are Roman or Byzantine, dating to roughly 1,500 to 2,000 years ago.

Inside, archaeologists recorded around eighteen well-preserved flat-bottomed containers, the kind used to carry liquids such as oil or wine. Some bear fine etched markings whose meaning is still unknown. A study published earlier this year suggests the vessel was heading west when it sank, in an area where strong currents and wind can be dangerous.

Culture minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy shared underwater footage of the site on social media, saying the find sheds light on long-running maritime trade along Anatolia's coasts. He framed it as part of an ongoing effort to protect underwater cultural heritage for future generations. The discovery matters because it pushes back the known record of seafaring in the region and offers a rare, largely intact snapshot of early Bronze Age trade.

title: Teaching students to think and learn through questions
summary: For Teachers' Day, OpenAI brings AI for Educators to Brazilian Portuguese and shows how Study Mode can help teachers take students through a problem step by step, asking questions rather than giving answers.
long_summary:
OpenAI marks Teachers' Day by honouring educators and the role good questions play in shaping a lesson. A campaign set in a university classroom takes a light-hearted look at how the relationship between teachers and students is changing, and it presents educators as essential in a world where AI is common.

OpenAI is launching its AI for Educators course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, its free learning platform. The course is aimed at teachers in primary, secondary and higher education. It shows how AI can help with planning lessons, creating activities and assessments, and drafting communications, while keeping the teacher's professional judgment in charge.

The article also promotes Study Mode, a feature in ChatGPT that a user can turn on from the tools menu. Rather than handing over answers, it guides learners through a topic with questions, hints, explanations and checks on understanding. OpenAI says the feature was developed with teachers, scientists and pedagogy experts to encourage active participation and reflection on one's own reasoning. A biology student studying enzymes is given as an example, and teachers are encouraged to test the tool on subjects they know well.

One illustration describes a science lesson on evaporation, in which students explore why clothes dry on a line using Study Mode and then write their own explanations without the chat in front of them. The teacher can use those answers to see what the class needs to revisit. The article closes by inviting teachers to experiment with the course and the tool, framing technology as a way to open up learning while teachers remain the people who know their students and ask the most important questions.

title: Scientists vote to end leap seconds, redefining how the world keeps time
summary: Leap seconds are on their way out. Under a new “leap hour”, official time will be allowed to drift as much as a full hour from the Earth's rotation.
long_summary:
Delegates at the General Conference on Weights and Measures in Versailles voted to end the leap second, the one-second adjustment that keeps Coordinated Universal Time, the world's standard clock, close to the planet's rotation. The change takes effect in May 2027, and the timescale will become continuous.

Instead of frequent corrections, time will be allowed to drift further from Earth's rotation, up to an hour, before a larger "leap hour" is added. Scientists expect that adjustment to be needed only after more than a thousand years. Noël Dimarcq of France's National Center for Scientific Research, who chairs a consultative committee at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, described the decision as the end of a debate that had lasted about thirty years.

The push for change is practical. Earth's rotation has recently sped up, raising the prospect of a negative leap second as early as 2029. Engineers warn that removing a second could disrupt computers, networks and navigation systems. Nick Stamatakos, who heads the Earth Orientation Department at the U.S. Naval Observatory, which manages the country's GPS timing, said avoiding negative leap seconds was a major reason for the change.

Most people will not notice the shift, and digital systems should benefit from avoiding sudden jumps in time. However, the change also weakens the link between official time and astronomical observation, a tie that goes back to humanity's earliest ways of measuring the day.

title: What would it take to terraform Mars? Erika DeBenedictis has ideas
summary: Erika DeBenedictis runs Pioneer Labs, a biotech start-up engineering microbes that could survive on Mars. Her goal is to turn alien worlds into places people could live, and she has ideas about what that would take.
long_summary:
Pioneer Labs, a nonprofit led by CEO Erika DeBenedictis, has announced what it calls the first microbe designed for Mars. Named sPL.001, it is an engineered version of a bacterium that naturally stores plastic, and it could in principle turn Martian soil, water and air into bioplastic for building astronaut habitats. The organism is designed to die if it escapes a sealed container, which lowers contamination risk. The team has also released papers on planetary protection, a reference architecture for biomanufacturing and a techno-economic analysis.

In the interview, DeBenedictis describes further microbes in development. One group is working on biologically produced transparent materials for greenhouses, while another is evolving organisms that can break down perchlorate, a toxic compound abundant in Martian dirt. The long-term aim is to make farmable land and eventually a greener, more Earth-like planet, though she calls terraforming a distant prospect. She argues that bringing a biosphere along is valuable for future human spaceflight, and that Mars, with its large buried ice deposits, is a promising target.

The interviewer raises three criticisms: why terraform, why Mars, and why now. Astrobiologists worry that introducing organisms could contaminate the planet and undermine the search for life. The interviewer also presses on the lack of peer review for the papers, which DeBenedictis attributes to the open-science policy of the Astera Institute, a backer of the work. She responds that peer review does not guarantee correctness, that colleagues have reviewed drafts, and that the papers aim to shape COSPAR and NASA's new M-FORCE group. Her proposed first flight test would use sPL.001 as a positive control in a search-for-life experiment.

title: Anthropic’s AI worm research raises new fears about smart device security
summary: Researchers looked at how an AI could spread itself through everyday smart gadgets, though cybersecurity experts say they've seen these tricks before.
long_summary:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published research on how AI models might spread as computer worms across cheap household devices. In their experiments, they split a small open-weight model from Google DeepMind's Gemma family across fifteen inexpensive TV boxes, with each box handling a few processing layers so the weak chips could collectively run the model. They also ran a sandboxed test in which a larger model from the Chinese start-up Z.ai got a smaller Meta Llama model running on target devices, though the larger model still depended on a separate server, so a fully self-sustaining worm was not demonstrated.

Jeffrey Ladish of Palisade Research, an AI safety nonprofit, argues the key lesson is that models can use any available computing resource, from laptops and data centers to smart TVs, once attackers gain access. Cybersecurity academics offer a more measured view. Michael Bailey of Georgia Tech warns against fearmongering, noting that self-replicating malware and botnets already exist. Vyas Sekar of Carnegie Mellon agrees the threats are classical, but says the bigger concern is that the barrier to launching such attacks is falling, which makes controlling data flow between smart devices more important.

The piece concludes that the novelty lies mainly in AI's ability to adapt and redistribute itself, while the underlying weakness is old: many connected gadgets are already easy to hijack, as past cryptocurrency mining takeovers show. The story matters because it highlights security gaps in everyday hardware that could become more dangerous as capable models shrink enough to run on it.

title: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 Review
summary: An old-school first-person shooter with two heroes and a campaign worth replaying, Boltgun 2 turns up the gory action of the Warhammer universe.
long_summary:
This is a review of Boltgun 2, a first-person shooter sequel from developer Auroch Digital set in Games Workshop's Warhammer 40,000 universe. The game keeps the fast, gory, old-school run-and-gun style of the original. The story begins with the player's ship being destroyed by a daemon, and the protagonist sets out on a bloody revenge campaign through hostile environments, clearing hordes of heretics while managing ammunition and health.

The sequel adds a second playable hero, a Sister of Battle, alongside the returning Space Marine. Each has different weapons and combat moves, and the reviewer finds both distinct and enjoyable. Branching level choices, varied mission objectives, four difficulty settings and accessibility options add to the replay value. The reviewer praises the retro art style, the detailed enemy designs and the voice performances by Rahul Kohli and Alanah Pearce.

The review also points out flaws. The structure can feel repetitive, and the story is sometimes muddled. Enemies occasionally stop fighting and wander idly, Purges sometimes fail to end, leaving the player stuck waiting for an exit that never unlocks, and movement can feel slippery during the harder platforming sections. The reviewer treats these as annoying rather than game-breaking.

Overall, the reviewer finds the combat, spectacle and atmosphere compelling and considers the game a worthwhile addition to the Warhammer universe. The mix of action, variety and replayability outweighs the technical problems in their view.

title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Review
summary: The long-awaited return of Castlevania brings the series up to date with fast, action-first play.
long_summary:
This review assesses Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, a new entry in Konami's long-running series built by Evil Empire, the studio behind the Return to Castlevania expansion for Dead Cells. The game is set in Paris, about 23 years after Castlevania III, and follows Rose Belmont, daughter of Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades. Trevor sends her to investigate a crisis, and her journey over roughly 10 to 15 hours leads to a familiar goal: defeating Dracula again. The reviewer finds the plot entertaining, with some clever twists tied to tarot cards Sypha left behind, though story is not what makes the series appealing.

Rose is praised as a strong, slightly rough-edged heroine who avoids being a passive character. Her allies are the spirits of defeated bosses sealed in her tarot cards, which limits interaction. The reviewer misses living characters and a populated world, noting that the abandoned Paris setting feels empty.

The map is made up of large connected zones with convenient features such as fast travel between save rooms, map markers and completion trackers, though the fast-travel load time is slow. The whip is the centrepiece, letting Rose swing and pull herself toward enemies, and combat offers several weapon types. The enemy roster is smaller than in earlier games, and some classic foes are absent.

The reviewer concludes that the game is enjoyable but feels more like a capable metroidvania with a Castlevania look than a traditional entry. Subweapons, RPG systems and familiar Belmont tools are largely gone, so fans hoping for a classic revival may come away disappointed.

title: Cartoon: America’s gargantuan debt
summary: A cartoon on America's enormous national debt, for a lighter look at the week's news.
